name: William McKinley
role: US president (1897-1901), congressman and governor of Ohio
summary: A Republican protectionist who wrote the 1890 McKinley Tariff, defended the gold standard and signed the Dingley Tariff. As president he led the war with Spain and annexed Hawaii and the Philippines, while calling for action against trusts and supporting labor arbitration and the voting rights of Black Southerners.

property-fundamental.rationale: The December 1900 message set Philippine rules that no person be deprived of property without due process and that private property not be taken without just compensation.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Called trusts and combinations that stifle competition and set prices obnoxious to the public welfare and urged Congress to check them under existing law. His 1897 inaugural endorsed the party stand against combinations of capital in trusts.

empower-police-military.rationale: Raised the regular army to its authorized maximum in 1898 and in his annual messages said the Secretary of War's recommendation for a permanent increase of the army had his unqualified approval.

more-religion-public.rationale: An Auxiliary to Religion, 1892, pp. 606–608, praises expanding Christian associations as strengthening citizenship and free institutions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: In the 1880s he praised Republican platforms against indiscriminate immigration, his inaugural urged further improving immigration and naturalization laws and his messages asked for amendment of the alien contract law, while his speeches also welcomed those fleeing despotism. Mixed evidence.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Inferred: from his repeated support for international arbitration as the true way of settling differences and his sending delegates to the 1899 peace conference; arbitration there was voluntary.

free-trade.rationale: Opposed free trade and revenue tariffs throughout his career, citing the 1846 revenue tariff as the cause of the 1857 collapse and endorsing the claim that free trade lowers wages. His later reciprocity policy was limited to exchanges that would not harm domestic industry.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: His April 1898 war message justified forcible intervention in Cuba first in the cause of humanity, to end barbarities, bloodshed and starvation, and rejected the argument that it was none of the US's business.

open-borders.rationale: The first inaugural advocates closing entry to those he describes as hostile to American institutions and adding immigration safeguards.

revolution-justified.rationale: July Fourth at Lakeside, pp. 583–584, celebrates the American Revolution as a justified struggle against oppression for self-government.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Authored the 1890 McKinley Tariff and signed the Dingley Tariff of 1897. In House speeches he argued that protection secures American industry and wages and that free trade ignores the welfare of workingmen.

one-party-rule.rationale: Issues Make Parties, 1892, pp. 574–575, says competing political parties are necessary and enduring agents of popular government.

war-builds-character.rationale: Buffalo speech: 'our real eminence rests in the victories of peace, not those of war'; the second inaugural hoped the nation might be spared the horrors of war.

separate-church-state.rationale: July Fourth at Lakeside, p. 584, endorses absolute separation; his 1900 Philippine instructions personally require complete church–state separation.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: In his 1897 annual message he said the treaty system under which the Five Civilized Tribes governed the Indian Territory had become impossible to continue and endorsed ending their trust and tribal government by Congress.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Annexed Hawaii by joint resolution, took the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam in the peace treaty with Spain, and defended expansion as duty and opportunity in his 1898-1899 speeches.

bound-labor.rationale: The American Workingman, 1891, p. 558, celebrates abolition of slave labor and workers’ freedom to enter voluntary employment.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: The 1897 and 1899 messages stressed that revenues should equal expenditures and that bond issues to cover deficits should be avoided.

national-self-determination.rationale: Pointed both ways: he said Cuba's government should be left to its people and Hawaii asked to be annexed, but the Philippines were placed under US sovereignty.

reason-over-faith.rationale: An Auxiliary to Religion, p. 607, says religion is indispensable to human flourishing and has no substitute.

class-collaboration.rationale: In a House speech supporting labor arbitration he called it the true way of settling differences between labor and capital, bringing them to better understanding and uniting them closer in interest.

national-mission.rationale: Said the liberators would not become oppressors and asked whether the country should sit in isolation and recognize no obligation to peoples whose conditions it had helped make. He spoke of spreading liberty rather than a mission to export its form of government as such.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: His inaugural said equality of rights must prevail and that lynchings must not be tolerated. His Equal Suffrage speech called the suppression of Black voters a new slavery. His policy toward Filipinos did not follow the same principle.

trade-surplus.rationale: Buffalo speech: wanted an outlet abroad for surplus production, but also said the country should take products from customers that it can use and should not sell everything while buying little; points both ways.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The Buffalo speech describes commercial competition as indispensable to advances in agriculture, industry and business.

separated-powers.rationale: The first inaugural recognizes Congress’s exclusive revenue power and the executive’s obligation to convene it to address fiscal needs.

party-controls-media.rationale: The first inaugural, collection p. 9, expressly commits to preserving and strengthening a free press.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Described the peoples of different Philippine islands as having different degrees of civilization and spoke of the degree of culture and advancement within their reach, treating advancement as differing between peoples.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The second inaugural welcomed the elected Cuban convention framing a constitution, and the 1898 message called for a government 'created by the people of Cuba'.

ban-cartels.rationale: In his 1899 annual message he said combinations to stifle competition, limit production and fix prices needed a remedy and that existing law should be extended to check monopolies without delay. He did not propose breaking up large firms as such.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: His protectionism aimed at a domestic market, but in 1901 he said the period of exclusiveness is past, that the country should buy abroad what it can use without harm to industry, and that commercial wars are unprofitable. He did not advocate a closed bloc.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: His 1898 proclamation described US rule of the Philippines as benevolent assimilation, and he said the US had an obligation to give a struggling people a better government and could not shift the new care.

patriotic-education.rationale: Children’s exercises and school speeches in the presidential collection praise teaching love of country, its flag and national hymns.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The December 1900 message set 'inviolable rules' for Philippine government, including due process and just compensation, which limit what government may do.

elective-rulers.rationale: July Fourth at Lakeside, pp. 583–584, celebrates replacing inherited sovereignty with self-government by the people.

office-by-exam.rationale: Said as president that civil service reforms must go on and that he had voted and spoken for the civil service law in Congress, which uses competitive examination. His record is mixed because he also loosened some rules; the statement also contrasts exams with election.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The first inaugural expressly says Congress alone can provide government revenue.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The first inaugural, presidential collection p. 9, treats respect for and obedience to law as a civic obligation.

non-intervention.rationale: Argued that the US had a duty to intervene in Cuba despite it being another nation's territory, and carried out the intervention.

religious-nation.rationale: Catholic Summer School address, August 1899, pp. 209–210, expressly defines national unity across different religious beliefs.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: His instructions on the Philippines said administration should be for the greatest good of the governed, while open to American trade; his critics said otherwise. Mixed evidence.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Inferred: his first inaugural derives presidential authority from the people’s will and constitutional oath, while invoking God’s guidance.

property-franchise.rationale: Equal Suffrage, pp. 165–180, defends equal voting rights for poor and rich citizens rather than a property qualification.

racial-franchise.rationale: Defended the right of Black citizens in the South to vote in his 1880s-1890 speeches, calling suppression of the ballot wicked, and supported the Federal Election Bill that provided federal supervision of elections.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Inferred: the 1892 YMCA address, pp. 606–607, connects physical, moral and religious development with sound citizenship and free institutions.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Asked Congress for authority to intervene by force in Cuba on humanitarian and interest grounds, and fought the Philippine War. Spain declared war after the US blockade.

arms-reduction.rationale: The 1899 message recorded that the United States had advocated disarmament at the Hague conference; he also sought a larger navy, so the answer is low.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Labor Arbitration, pp. 196–199, supports organized workers and employers jointly settling wages and disputes through voluntary arbitration.

notes:
Positions come from his House speeches (1878-1891), first inaugural, annual messages and 1898-1901 speeches. Many topics he never addressed are null. His second-term stance on tariffs softened toward reciprocity in the Buffalo speech.

claude-haiku-5-5 notes: Only the Second Inaugural (1901), the 1898 war message, the Buffalo speech (1901), the annual messages of 1897 to 1900 and the 1898 Philippine proclamation were read in full. Not retrieved: the first inaugural (1897), the McKinley Tariff (1890) and his tariff speeches, and any text on the Gold Standard Act of 1900 itself. The 1899 message urged keeping the gold standard, but no statement in the test covers gold or currency, so none is answered. The reported remarks to Methodist ministers (1899) could not be checked against a primary text and are not used. Most answers rest on his messages and the Buffalo speech, so statements about labour, immigration, race, religion and social issues are null because his opening speeches and messages did not address them. Public web search was exhausted during the audit, so tariff-speech and first-inaugural sources are missing.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent third audit, no prior answers copied. Full texts of both speech collections and all four annual messages downloaded; searched each thin theme and reviewed all 490 statement texts. Religion table: the Lakeside address supplies an explicit church–state separation position; YMCA address supports a public religious role; Catholic Summer School speech supplies a civic definition of national belonging. Divine-source-of-authority and spiritual-nature are explicitly limited historical inferences, not direct theological claims. No evidence for scriptural civil law, blasphemy penalties, premarital-sex doctrine, party command of the army or revolutionary vanguard politics. Public-school neutrality and general church–state separation do not, by themselves, settle all religious instruction in state schools: no-religion-state-schools remains null. His commission’s later education regulations are not automatically attributed to him. No secondhand Rusling Philippines-prayer account is used. Equal Suffrage is about Black male voting rights, not evidence for women’s suffrage. Religious addresses include quotations from Washington and Lincoln; separate speakers’ words are not treated as new McKinley testimony except where he expressly endorses their principles. 1897 non-aggression pledges are superseded by his personally driven expansion and wars. Reciprocity at Buffalo softened exclusiveness but did not renounce protective tariffs. His civil-service promises were checked against later exemptions, so no unqualified meritocracy answer is assigned. Forest-reserve administration was examined but does not establish intrinsic value of nature, degrowth or other unrelated ecological doctrines. Eight-hour federal-employment advocacy is not generalized into a policy on all private employment. War authorization is not treated as extralegal political violence.
